\vspace{-1.2em}

\noindent\textbf{In one paragraph.} \code{lutorch\_ex} is a small PyTorch library for \emph{lookup-table layers}: a
learnable map built from many discrete tables, each addressed by a cheap locality-sensitive hash of its
input. It has four parts, and this report walks through them in order: the tables and their hash
(\S\ref{sec:idea}); a projection wrapper that gives a stack of tables an ordinary vector-in, vector-out
interface, so it can sit anywhere a feed-forward layer would (\S\ref{sec:projection}); \emph{cartridges}
--- interchangeable read mathematics behind
one fixed contract, in three generations (\S\ref{sec:cartridges}--\ref{sec:body}), one of which is
quantised to int8 and ships with a deployment path (\S\ref{sec:quant}--\ref{sec:deploy}); and the shared
machinery of regularisers, precision and kernels (\S\ref{sec:machinery}). \S\ref{sec:ml} reports a
seven-configuration sweep at 48k steps; \S\ref{sec:status} lists what is still open. Reference material
is in Appendix~\ref{app:ref}.

% ======================================================================================================
\section{The idea: tables addressed by an LSH}
\label{sec:idea}

A lookup table (LUT) replaces a multiply-accumulate with an \emph{address} and a \emph{read}. Hash the
input to a small integer with a locality-sensitive hash (LSH) --- here, a handful of sign bits --- and
fetch the stored vector at that address. The construction comes from Izhikevich's \emph{Spiking
Manifesto}~\citep{manifesto}: a spiking network stores a vast number of synapses but touches only those of
the neurons that fired, which is exactly what a table read does, and the \emph{order} of spikes rather than
their magnitude carries the information, which is exactly what a sign-bit address encodes.

\paragraph{One table.} Work in a space $z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_\text{in}}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:table}). An
\emph{anchor} is an index into $z$. A table owns \code{nap} \emph{probes}; probe $j$ is either an anchor
pair $(a_j,b_j)$, giving $u_j=z[a_j]-z[b_j]$, or a single anchor $a_j$, giving $u_j=z[a_j]$. Each probe
contributes one bit $[\,u_j>0\,]$, so an address $c\in[0,K)$ has \code{nap} bits and the table has
$K=2^{\text{nap}}$ cells, each holding a learnable row $W[c]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_\text{out}}$. The magnitudes $|u_j|$ are the
\emph{margins}: how far each bit is from flipping. The smallest one, $u^\star=\min_j|u_j|$, marks the
least certain bit, and flipping that bit gives the \emph{neighbour} cell $c'$ --- the one the input would
land in under the smallest perturbation. Every read mathematics in this library --- every
\emph{cartridge}, in the vocabulary of \S\ref{sec:cartridges} --- uses $c$, $u$, and $c'$ and nothing else
from the input.

\paragraph{Two kinds of probe.} Which kind a layer uses is fixed when the layer is built. In the default,
pair form, every probe compares two coordinates of $z$: this is the manifesto's Eq.~1, where the bit
records which of two neurons fired first. In the single form every probe tests the sign of one
coordinate instead.

\paragraph{Many tables, many heads.} A layer stacks \code{tph} tables per group over $G$ groups, called
heads. A head reads its own slice of the input and writes its own slice of the output, and its output
is the \emph{sum} of its \code{tph} table reads (weighted, in some cartridges). A layer may also fan
several heads into one shared output by summing them.

% ======================================================================================================
\section{ProjectionLUT: input and output projections}
\label{sec:projection}

On its own a table reads a narrow per-group vector of a space whose axes it cannot choose.
\code{ProjectionMHL} (the ``ProjectionLUT'' wrapper, Figure~\ref{fig:projlut}) puts a plain linear map on
each side of the cartridge --- the stack of tables together with its read mathematics --- so that, from
the outside, it takes an ordinary vector of width $D_\text{in}$ and returns one of width $D_\text{out}$,
like any feed-forward layer, while the tables work in their narrow per-head spaces. The two widths are
independent arguments of the wrapper and may differ. Writing $h_\text{in}$ and $h_\text{out}$ for the number of input and output heads and $d_\text{in}$,
$d_\text{out}$ for their widths ($h_\text{in}=h_\text{out}=G$ in the usual per-head case\footnote{The two head counts
may differ only when one of them is $1$; the library rejects every other combination. With
$h_\text{in}=1$ the input projection produces one $d_\text{in}$-wide slice that all $G$ heads read
(fan-out); with $h_\text{out}=1$ the heads' outputs are summed into one $d_\text{out}$-wide slice that
the output projection consumes (fan-in).}):
\[
  x\in[B,D_\text{in}]\ \xrightarrow{\ \code{compress}\ }\ z\in[B,h_\text{in},d_\text{in}]
  \ \xrightarrow{\ \code{cartridge}\ }\ y\in[B,h_\text{out},d_\text{out}]
  \ \xrightarrow{\ \code{decompress}\ }\ \text{out}\in[B,D_\text{out}].
\]
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
\item \textbf{The input projection shapes the hashing.} A probe is also a hyperplane test, and what
  plane it tests depends on whether \code{compress} is in front and on the kind of probe:
  \begin{center}\footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{@{}l >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.9cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.6cm}@{}}
  \toprule
  & single anchors & anchor pairs \\
  \midrule
  \code{compress} off & $x[a]>0$: an axis-aligned plane of the raw input & $x[a]-x[b]>0$: coefficients $\pm1$, zero bias --- the manifesto's form \\
  \code{compress} on & $w_a^\top x+b_a>0$: an arbitrary learned hyperplane & $(w_a-w_b)^\top x+(b_a-b_b)>0$: also arbitrary; up to $\binom{d_\text{in}}{2}$ distinct planes per head \\
  \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}
  With \code{compress} on, a single-anchor probe reads one row of the projection and is exactly the
  manifesto's ``hyperplane LSH'' with learnable anchor vectors (\citealp[\S VIII-H]{manifesto}).
  With \code{compress} in front, both modes get arbitrary hyperplanes, but the same projection yields far
  more distinct planes in pair form, so tables stop re-using the same few bits; single anchors are
  somewhat weaker, though not dramatically. Without \code{compress} the gap is large: a single anchor only
  tests the sign of one raw coordinate, an axis-aligned split, where a pair still compares two.
\item \textbf{The output projection compresses the tables.} A layer holds an exponential number of
  cells --- \code{tph} tables per head, $K=2^{\text{nap}}$ cells each, times the heads, so the count is
  exponential in \code{nap} --- and every cell stores a $d_\text{out}$-wide row, so the per-cell width
  $d_\text{out}$ is what controls table size. For example, with 8 heads of 64 tables
  and \code{nap}$=8$ --- the geometry of the six-block language model of \S\ref{sec:ml} --- that is
  $8\times64\times256=131{,}072$ cells per layer, $6.3$M table parameters at $d_\text{out}=48$
  ($37.7$M over six layers, more than half of the model's $68.2$M); at the model width of $384$ it would
  be $50$M per layer. So the tables live in a narrow $d_\text{out}$ ($48$ in every experiment below), and
  \code{decompress} expands the summed read back to model width afterwards, at the cost of one small
  dense map per layer ($0.15$M parameters).
\end{itemize}
Given a learned input projection, the single-anchor mode alone would have sufficed in principle: a pair
comparison $z[a]-z[b]>0$ is itself a hyperplane on $x$, so anchor pairs could have been dropped and left
to \code{compress} to realise. The library keeps both modes deliberately. The pair comparison is the
Spiking Manifesto's mechanism as stated --- the relative order of two coordinates --- and it is the
cheap special case that the whole design is built to exploit: an address bit costs two coordinate reads
and one subtraction, with the anchors stored as integer indices and no weights of its own (the kernels
do exactly this), whereas a general per-table hyperplane would cost a $d_\text{in}$-length dot product and
$d_\text{in}$ weights per bit --- at the sweep geometry, some 4{,}000 subtractions per token and layer
against about 200{,}000 multiply-adds. Single anchors were added later for flexibility, as the even
cheaper probe, and sit at the other end of the same trade.

Either side may be switched off (Identity) when the widths already match. By default \code{decompress} is
initialised to zero and \code{compress} to $\mathcal{N}(0,0.02)$.

% ======================================================================================================
\section{Cartridges: one contract, three generations}
\label{sec:cartridges}

Everything described so far is the same for every read form: the geometry, the addressing, the sum over
tables, the routing, the wrapper. A
\emph{cartridge} is the swappable read \emph{mathematics} inside that frame. The contract is a shape:
$[B,h_\text{in},d_\text{in}]\to[B,h_\text{out},d_\text{out}]$ (\code{MultiHeadLUT}), and the wrapper never
reaches inside it. Every shipped cartridge inherits one base, \code{ManifestoLUT}, which owns the tables
$W\in\mathbb{R}^{G\times\text{tph}\times K\times d_\text{out}}$, the anchors (drawn once from a seed and
never trained), the addressing
$(c,\,u,\,c')$, the sum over \code{tph} and the routing; what a cartridge adds is how it turns the addressed
cell, its neighbour and the margins into a per-table output --- and which function training differentiates.

\paragraph{Three generations of one idea.} The cartridges form a progression. Gen-1 \emph{Manifesto} is
the Spiking Manifesto's model as published: a hard read and a fixed uncertainty function for the
gradient. Gen-2 \emph{SoftSign} replaces the fixed uncertainty by a blend weight with two learned
temperatures. Gen-3 \emph{Confidence} replaces the blend by a learned \emph{score} that weights each table
by how confident its address is --- and has an int8 twin for deployment. Table~\ref{tab:matrix} is the map.

\paragraph{Pure and fused twins.} Each generation has a \emph{pure} cartridge --- readable PyTorch, the
numerical oracle --- and a \emph{fused} twin with the same mathematics that dispatches each forward to the
fastest available path: a single \code{F.embedding\_bag} over the addressed cells, or co-located CUDA
kernels (\S\ref{sec:machinery}). Fused twins are tested against the pure ones; the sweep in
\S\ref{sec:ml} runs the fused twins where they exist.

% ======================================================================================================
\section{The cartridges}
\label{sec:body}

Each subsection follows one template: the value, the gradient, what is learned, when to use it, and the
three lines that build it. Throughout, \code{spec} is a \code{LUTSpec} --- the layer's geometry in one
frozen dataclass: heads, tables per head, probes per table, widths and probe kind
(Appendix~\ref{app:ref}) --- and \code{ffn = ProjectionMHL(cart, input\_dim=$D_\text{in}$,
output\_dim=$D_\text{out}$)} wraps any cartridge (\code{d\_model=}$D$ is the shorthand for
$D_\text{in}=D_\text{out}=D$).

\subsection{Manifesto: \code{ManifestoHardLUT}, \code{ManifestoSoftLUT}}
\label{sec:manifesto}
The Spiking Manifesto's model and learning rule, with its uncertainty function.

\textbf{Value.} The hard read $y=\sum_t W_t[c_t]$ --- one row per table, added, no multiply (manifesto
Eqs.~1--3). \textbf{Gradient.} The addresses are integers, so the paper differentiates a surrogate instead
(its Eq.~4): the two-cell blend
\[
  \tilde y=\sum_t\big[(1-U_t)\,W_t[c_t]+U_t\,W_t[c_t']\big],\qquad U_t=U(u^\star_t)=\frac{0.5}{1+|u^\star_t|},
\]
whose derivative lands on the two anchors of the deciding probe alone (Eq.~5):
$\partial\tilde y/\partial z[a]=-\partial\tilde y/\partial z[b]=U'(u^\star)\,(W[c']-W[c])$. $U$ is the paper's own choice; $U(0)=\tfrac12$,
$U\to0$ for a confident bit. \textbf{Learned:} the tables only.

\textbf{Hard vs.\ soft, and provenance.} \code{ManifestoHardLUT} is Izhikevich's rule verbatim: hard value
at train and eval, the addressed row updated, the input gradient through the minimal-pair surrogate Eq.~4
with $U=0.5/(1+|u|)$ (\citealp[\S III-A and Fig.~10]{manifesto}). \code{ManifestoSoftLUT} goes one step
beyond the paper: it uses Eq.~4 itself as the forward value at train \emph{and} eval, so both the addressed
cell and its neighbour receive weight gradient. The manifesto states that $U$ is used ``only in the training
mode to calculate gradients'' and that inference uses Eq.~3 without $U$ (\S III-A); its appendix explores
other surrogates of the same family --- all pairs, or dropping the flipped row, $y=\sum S_x(1-U)$
(\S VIII-K, Eqs.~17--18) --- again only as learning rules. In the sweep the soft read is the better of the
two by $0.012$ bpb (Table~\ref{tab:results}).

\textbf{Fused twins.} \code{FusedManifestoHardLUT} keeps the exact straight-through backward in a
hand-written scatter: the weight gradient goes to row $c$ by \code{index\_add}, the input gradient is
$U'(u^\star)$ times the alignment of the output gradient with $W[c]-W[c']$, scattered to the deciding pair
with opposite signs. \code{FusedManifestoSoftLUT} reads with \code{embedding\_bag} and per-sample weights
$[1-U,\,U]$. Both can route training to the native \code{lprojection} kernels. \textbf{When:} the
reference points; the hard read is the cheapest possible inference.
\begin{lstlisting}
from spiky.lutorch_ex import LUTSpec, FusedManifestoHardLUT, FusedManifestoSoftLUT, ProjectionMHL
spec = LUTSpec(h_in=8, h_out=8, tph=64, nap=8, d_in=48, d_out=48)
ffn  = ProjectionMHL(FusedManifestoSoftLUT(spec, seed=1), input_dim=384, output_dim=384)
\end{lstlisting}

\subsection{SoftSign: \code{SoftSignHardLUT}, \code{SoftSignSmoothLUT}}
\label{sec:softsign}
Gen-2 keeps Gen-1's structure and replaces the fixed $U$ by a blend weight with two learned temperatures
per layer (the two-cell form of the soft-sign mechanism in \citealp[\S2]{mechanisms}):
\[
  \rho=\frac{|u^\star|}{T_\text{soft}+|u^\star|}\in(0,1),\qquad
  w=\sigma\!\big(-2\rho/T_\text{sel}\big)\in(0,\tfrac12]\ \ \text{(weight on the neighbour $c'$)}.
\]
\textbf{Value / gradient.} \code{SoftSignHardLUT}: hard read, surrogate $(1-w)W[c]+w\,W[c']$ for the
input and the temperatures, weights updated on row $c$. \code{SoftSignSmoothLUT}: the blend is the value
at train and eval, both rows learn. Only the two cells $\{c,c'\}$ enter; a softmax over all $K$ cells and
several-neighbour forms are deliberately out of scope.
\textbf{Learned:} tables, $\log T_\text{soft}$, $\log T_\text{sel}$ (init $0.5$; freezable).
\textbf{Fused twins.} \code{FusedSoftSignHardLUT} runs its training step on the native kernels plus one
small surrogate-gradient kernel (a clear win: $1.6\times$ faster step, $2.7\times$ less memory than the pure
cartridge at the training batch); \code{FusedSoftSignSmoothLUT}'s best path is the \code{embedding\_bag}
one, so that is what its default dispatch picks. \textbf{When:} when a learned sharpness matters and
the score of Gen-3 is not wanted.
\begin{lstlisting}
ffn = ProjectionMHL(FusedSoftSignSmoothLUT(spec, seed=1, soft_score_temp=0.5, select_temp=0.5), input_dim=384, output_dim=384)
\end{lstlisting}

\subsection{Confidence: \code{ConfidenceLUT}}
\label{sec:confidence}
Gen-3 does not blend by uncertainty --- it \emph{weights} each table by how confident its address is,
with the learned-margin score of LookupFFN~\citep{lookupffn} (derived in \citealp[\S3, \S6]{mechanisms}).
With margins $m_j=|u_j|$,
\[
  s=\Big(\sum_j m_j\Big)\exp\!\Big(\gamma\sum_j\log\sigma(\beta m_j)\Big),\qquad
  \beta=e^{\log\beta},\ \gamma=e^{\log\gamma}\ \text{learned per layer (init $2,1$)}.
\]
\textbf{Value.} $n{=}1$: $y=\sum_t s_t\,W_t[c_t]$. $n{=}2$: the scored two-cell blend
$y=\sum_t s_t\big[(1-v_t)W_t[c_t]+v_t\,W_t[c_t']\big]$ with $v=\sigma(-2|u^\star|/\tau)\in(0,\tfrac12]$
the weight on the \emph{neighbour}\footnote{The code and the ablation table write $v$ on the neighbour,
$v=\sigma(-2|u^\star|/\tau)$. The quantisation note~\citep{quantnote} writes the same blend the other way,
$v=\sigma(2u^\star/\tau)$ on the addressed cell; the values agree since $\sigma(x)+\sigma(-x)=1$.}, $\tau$
learned per layer (init $0.5$). \textbf{Gradient.} The value itself. The address is a detached integer, so
the input gradient reaches $z$ \emph{only} through $s$ (all \code{nap} margins) and, for $n{=}2$, through
$v$ (the deciding margin): a table learns how confident to be, never that a different row would have been
better. \textbf{Learned:} tables, $\log\beta$, $\log\gamma$, and $\log\tau$ for $n{=}2$.
\textbf{Implementation.} One \code{embedding\_bag} with the scores as per-sample weights; the whole
training forward is \code{torch.compile}d on CUDA, which folds the score's chain of small kernels and is
what makes this cartridge's training step the cheapest of the three (\S\ref{sec:bench}). \textbf{When:} the best
accuracy of the three generations (Table~\ref{tab:results}); fp32/fp64 only.
\begin{lstlisting}
cart = ConfidenceLUT(spec, seed=1, read_top_n=2, beta_init=2.0, gamma_init=1.0,
                     read_tau_init=0.5, read_tau_learnable=True)
ffn  = ProjectionMHL(cart, input_dim=384, output_dim=384)
\end{lstlisting}

\subsection{Quantised confidence: \code{QuantisedConfidenceLUT}}
\label{sec:quant}
The same cartridge trained so that the deployed read needs only int8 rows, additions and bit shifts
(\code{quant\_mode="p2\_int8"}; the derivation is \citealp{quantnote}, here only the three facts).
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep1pt
\item \textbf{Rows are int8 with a power-of-two scale} shared by all tables of a group and one output
  channel: $e_{g,k}=\lceil\log_2\max|W|\rceil-7$, $\hat W=\operatorname{clamp}(\operatorname{round}(W/2^{e}),-128,127)$.
  Training uses $2^{e}\hat W$ in value with a straight-through gradient to the float master $W$.
\item \textbf{The two blend weights are rounded to powers of two.} With $r=(1-v)/v=e^{-2|u^\star|/\tau}$
  the read factorises as $s(1-v)\,(W[c]+r\,W[c'])$; $q=\operatorname{round}(2|u^\star|/(\tau\ln2))$ rounds
  $r$ to $2^{-q}$ and $k'=\operatorname{round}(\log_2 s-c_q)$ rounds the rest, so a table contributes
  $2^{k'}W[c]+2^{k'-q}W[c']$. Again straight-through: the forward uses the rounded weights, the gradient
  is that of $s(1-v)$ and $s\,v$, so $\beta,\gamma,\tau$ keep learning.
\item \textbf{The integer read.} In units of $2^{-6}$ every shift is a left shift, the int32 sum fits, and
  the per-$(g,k)$ scale $2^{e-6}$ is the only float left --- and it is applied \emph{after} the table sum.
\end{enumerate}
Exact constants (window, cutoffs, drop rule) are in Table~\ref{tab:quant} of the appendix. The train-mode
read equals the deployed read bit for bit; \code{forward\_int} performs the int32 shift-add for
cross-checking. \textbf{Cost:} $+0.0012$ bpb against the float cartridge in the 48k sweep, under the
$+0.003$ upper bound of the note; tables $4\times$ smaller. \textbf{When:} whenever the model will be
deployed. $n{=}2$ is the reference integer form; $n{=}1$ is a library extension.
\begin{lstlisting}
cart = QuantisedConfidenceLUT(spec, seed=1, quant_mode="p2_int8", read_top_n=2,
                              beta_init=2.0, gamma_init=1.0, read_tau_init=0.5)
\end{lstlisting}

\subsection{Deployment: the \code{.lxq} format}
\label{sec:deploy}
\begin{lstlisting}
from spiky.lutorch_ex import export_deployment, load_deployment
export_deployment(model, "m.lxq")                                   # int8 rows, scale folded, fp32 dropped
dep = load_deployment("m.lxq", make_skeleton, device="cuda").eval()  # the fp32 table is never allocated
\end{lstlisting}
\code{export\_deployment} walks the model and, for every \code{ProjectionMHL} whose cartridge emits a
compact payload (\code{to\_deployment()}, a protocol the base answers with ``dense, nothing to do''),
writes the int8 rows, the anchors and the three scalars, and \textbf{folds the scale $2^{e-6}$ into a copy
of that layer's \code{decompress} weight}. The fold is exact --- a power of two only touches the exponent
field of a float --- and legal because nothing sits between the table sum and \code{decompress} and one
exponent is shared across a group's tables, so it factors out of the sum (the same idea as the
\code{SupportsDecompressBake} hook of the wrapper, applied once and statically at export; the runtime
hook is implemented by no shipped cartridge). The loader builds the architecture on the \code{meta}
device, rebuilds each compacted layer from a format tag through a small registry (so \code{deploy.py}
names no cartridge class), and loads the rest of the state dict. The deployed cartridge holds only the
int8 \code{packed} buffer and returns the raw int32 accumulator; the file is a safetensors container with
a JSON header. Per layer at the sweep geometry: 24~MiB fp32 $\to$ 6~MiB int8. Scope today: $n{=}2$ and
$h_\text{out}=G$.

% ======================================================================================================
\section{Shared machinery}
\label{sec:machinery}

\paragraph{Regularisers (both default off, inherited by every cartridge).} \emph{Cell total variation}:
view a table's $K=2^{\text{nap}}$ cells as the vertices of an \code{nap}-cube and penalise the mean squared
difference over all Hamming-1 pairs, $\mathcal R_\text{TV}=\langle\|W_c-W_{c'}\|_2^2\rangle_{(c,c')}$
(the mean over the $n_\text{tables}\cdot\text{nap}\cdot2^{\text{nap}-1}$ pairs) --- a locality prior: a
one-bit address flip should change the read little. \code{cell\_tv\_penalty(model)}
averages it over the model's cartridges; add $\lambda\,\mathcal R_\text{TV}$ to the loss. \emph{Table
dropout} (\code{table\_dropout\_rate}): inverted dropout at whole-table granularity, one Bernoulli per
(sample, group, table), training only; a dropped table contributes nothing to the value or the gradient.

\paragraph{Precision.} The pure cartridges are fp32/fp64 and raise on bf16/fp16. The fused Manifesto and
SoftSign twins accept bf16/fp16: addressing runs in fp32 (so a lossy margin cannot flip a bit), reads and
reductions accumulate in fp32, the output is cast once. Gen-3 is fp32/fp64.

\paragraph{Compilation and kernels.} Eval forwards are \code{torch.compile}d on CUDA; training forwards
are compiled only for Gen-3, where it pays. The fused twins resolve one native extension,
\code{lutorch\_ex\_lprojection} (the lookup and anchor-pair kernels under \code{cartridges/csrc/},
JIT-built with \code{torch.utils.cpp\_extension}), plus three small standalone kernels (int8 scalars,
single-anchor input gradient, soft-sign surrogate). Each is lazy, cached across processes, and falls back
to pure torch on CPU or without \code{nvcc}/\code{ninja}, with identical results. A \code{backend=}
argument forces \code{pure}, \code{tier1} or \code{native} on any fused twin; \code{bench.py} times the
forward, training forward and backward of any configuration.

% ======================================================================================================
\section{Experiments: the seven-configuration sweep}
\label{sec:ml}

\paragraph{Setup.} A six-block GPT ($d_\text{model}=384$, 6 attention heads, $68.2$M parameters) with the
feed-forward layer of every block replaced by a \code{ProjectionMHL} around the cartridge under test.
Every configuration here is square: the wrapper's input and output widths both equal the model width,
$D_\text{in}=D_\text{out}=d_\text{model}=384$. All
seven runs share the champion topology --- $h_\text{in}=h_\text{out}=8$, \code{tph}$=64$, \code{nap}$=8$,
$d_\text{in}=d_\text{out}=48$, anchor pairs --- seed~1, the default init (per-head Uniform$[\pm10^{-3}]$
tables, \code{decompress} zeroed), cell-TV
$\lambda=10$, table dropout $0.2$, AdamW ($3\!\times\!10^{-4}$, weight decay $0.1$, none on the tables),
48{,}000 steps, cosine schedule with $10\%$ warm-up to a $0.1\times$ floor, sequence length 512, 24{,}576
tokens per step (device batch 12, accumulation 4), evaluation every 500 steps; the backbone runs in bf16,
the LUT layers in fp32. Data and tokenisation are the \emph{NanoChat} setup: the ClimbMix text corpus as
prepared by nanochat's data script, streamed and tokenised on the fly by nanochat's RustBPE tokenizer
(32{,}768-entry vocabulary, trained by nanochat on the same corpus) into BOS-aligned 512-token rows;
\code{val\_bpb} is the validation cross-entropy in bits divided by the number of \emph{bytes} of the
decoded text (nanochat's bits-per-byte evaluation on a fixed held-out set), so it is comparable across
tokenisers. Per-run configs, metric histories and summaries are under \code{experiments/lutorch\_ex/}.

\paragraph{Reading the results.} Four things are visible in Table~\ref{tab:results} and
Figure~\ref{fig:curves}. (i) A \emph{soft} read beats its hard counterpart in every generation: $-0.012$
(Manifesto), $-0.027$ (SoftSign), $-0.011$ (Confidence $n{=}2$ vs.\ $n{=}1$). (ii) A \emph{learned
confidence score} beats a blend by uncertainty: the Confidence line leads the SoftSign line by $0.023$ and
the Manifesto line by $0.033$. The two effects stack, and the ordering is fixed from about step 8k
onwards. (iii) \emph{Quantisation is nearly free}: int8 rows and power-of-two weights cost $+0.0012$ bpb,
well under the $+0.003$ bound of the quantisation note, for tables one quarter the size. (iv) Against the
dense feed-forward layer, the two scored two-cell cartridges \emph{win} ($-0.009$ and $-0.008$ bpb), the
single-cell scored read is within $0.002$, and the blend-only generations trail by $0.014$--$0.041$; the
LUT models carry $1.9\times$ the parameters of the dense one, but a LUT layer touches only two 48-wide rows
per table per token.

\subsection{Benchmarks: CPU, RTX 5090, H100}
\label{sec:bench}
Table~\ref{tab:bench} times the layer alone, at the sweep geometry, for the seven optimised configurations
the sweep used: the four fused twins and the three Gen-3 configurations (whose \code{embedding\_bag} +
compiled forward is already the optimised path; the pure reference cartridges are not benchmarked). The
CPU and RTX 5090 columns were measured for this report with the library's own harness (\code{bench.py},
driven by \code{bench\_report.py} next to this report); the H100 column is carried over from the
benchmark recorded in the pull request that landed the Gen-3 cartridges\footnote{PR \#138, the
``full cross-generation benchmark'' comment, commit \code{996046ce}: H100 80\,GB, fp32, each cartridge in
its own process, 25 warm-up + 60 timed repetitions, GPU clock held at 1980\,MHz. PR \#137 reports the
four fused Gen-1/2 twins on the same card with the same harness and agrees within 2\%. Those recorded
numbers are process-peak allocations; the RTX 5090 peak here is the allocation added by one training
step. The deployed int8 cartridge (\S\ref{sec:deploy}) has no training row; its recorded eval forward
(PR \#139, H100, $B=4{,}096$) was 2.6\,ms against 2.8\,ms for the float twin.}, and is not re-measured
here --- that machine is gone.

native kernels active): medians of 10 repeats after 3 warm-ups; CPU (24-thread desktop part, the fused
twins' \code{embedding\_bag} path, $B=1{,}024$): medians of 15 repeats after 5 warm-ups, with the
fastest repeat within $15\%$ of the median (the committed \code{bench\_cpu.json} and

\label{tab:bench}

Three readings. On either GPU the training step of every blend or hard cartridge is $20$--$29$ ms at the
training batch and is dominated by the backward ($17$--$19$ ms), the scatter into the $6.3$M-entry table;
\code{ConfidenceLUT} $n{=}1$ is both the cheapest step ($11.5$ ms) and the smallest footprint ($1.1$
GB), because its compiled forward fuses the score's chain of small kernels and reads one cell. Reading two
cells ($n{=}2$, the soft forms) roughly doubles the eval forward ($1.0\to3.5$ ms for Manifesto,
$1.5\to4.6$ ms for Confidence). The quantised cartridge's eval forward is not faster than the float one
--- its training-time read still fetches float rows for the straight-through estimator; the integer read
belongs to the deployed cartridge (\S\ref{sec:deploy}). The two GPUs agree to within $15\%$ on every row:
these layers are bound by memory traffic, not arithmetic. On the CPU, at a batch $24\times$ smaller, the
same layers take $36$--$92$ ms per step --- roughly two orders of magnitude slower per row --- with the
same ordering: the one-cell scored read is the cheapest, the two-cell blends cost $1.7$--$2.6\times$ more.

% ======================================================================================================
\section{Status and what is next}
\label{sec:status}
\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
\item \textbf{One seed.} Every row of Table~\ref{tab:results}, the dense baseline included, is a single
  seed; differences below about $0.003$ bpb are inside seed noise at this scale.
\item \textbf{Single-anchor mode} (\S\ref{sec:idea}) is implemented and tested for every cartridge but none
  of the seven runs uses it.
\item \textbf{Deployment} covers $n{=}2$ and $h_\text{out}=G$ only; fan-in would need a pre-route scale.
  int4 is defined by the quantisation note but untested in this library.
\item \textbf{Benchmarks} (\S\ref{sec:bench}) are single-process microbenchmarks of the layer alone; an
  end-to-end training-throughput and inference-latency measurement of the whole model is still to do.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Environment and layout.} \sloppy \code{LUTORCH\_EX\_NO\_COMPILE=1} disables
\code{torch.compile}, \code{LUTORCH\_EX\_NO\_CUDA\_EXT=1} skips the JIT kernels, \code{TORCH\_EXTENSIONS\_DIR}
relocates their build cache. Under \code{src/spiky/lutorch\_ex/}: the geometry, contract, addressing,
anchors, wrapper, deployment and benchmark modules at the top level; one module per cartridge under
\code{cartridges/} (shared base \code{manifesto\_base.py}, quantisation mathematics \code{\_pow2.py},
kernel sources \code{csrc/}); 17 test files under \code{tests/}.

\end{document}
